body.stem: Your team owns a budget in a development subscription, configured as shown below. You need to work out which amount one month's accumulated cost is measured against, so that you can interpret a threshold breach correctly. Which amount applies to a single month of the current quarter?

explanation.correct: With a quarterly reset period, the configured amount is spread evenly across the three months of the quarter, so 12,000 USD gives each month a share of 4,000 USD. The cost being tracked restarts at zero at the start of every new period, which is why the 80% threshold of this budget fires at 3,200 USD of monthly spend.

perChoice.b: That is the total for the entire quarter. It is the figure the three monthly shares add up to, not the amount a single month is measured against.
perChoice.c: Spreading an amount across twelve months applies to an annual reset period. A quarterly budget divides its amount across the three months of the quarter, so this figure is too low.
perChoice.d: Nothing is split in half at the middle of a quarter; the amount is divided evenly across the three months, so no month is measured against this figure.

body.stem: You are reviewing a shutdown recommendation in Advisor for an idle virtual machine. You need to confirm which signals Advisor uses before it proposes turning that machine off, so you can explain the recommendation to your team. Which metrics does Advisor evaluate for shutdown recommendations?

columns: Observation for the last seven days
rows: No incoming requests, no outbound traffic reported
P95 of maximum CPU utilization across all cores
P100 of average CPU utilization over the last three days

options.text: CPU and Outbound Network utilization
CPU and memory utilization
Memory and Outbound Network utilization
Disk throughput and CPU utilization

explanation.correct: For shutdown recommendations, Advisor analyzes CPU and Outbound Network utilization, which it has found to be sufficient signals. A shutdown recommendation is raised when the CPU and network values stay under the low-utilization thresholds over the last seven days, matching the flat metrics shown for the machine.

perChoice.b: Memory is deliberately excluded from shutdown recommendations. Advisor evaluates CPU and Outbound Network utilization for this recommendation type.
perChoice.c: Although Outbound Network utilization is one signal, memory is not part of the shutdown criteria, so pairing them is incorrect.
perChoice.d: Disk throughput is not one of the metrics Advisor uses for shutdown recommendations; the criteria are CPU and Outbound Network utilization.

body.stem: You applied the Advisor recommendation below to vm-app-03, then compared the next invoice with the estimate. The drop in spend was far smaller than the figure Advisor displayed. You need to explain the gap to the finance team. Which statement from the Advisor cost recommendations accounts for it?

rows: Reserved Instances held in the subscription

options.text: The listed saving is worked out with retail rates and ignores Reserved Instances and Savings plan purchases
The listed saving already deducts Reserved Instances and Savings plan purchases, so your coverage is built in
The listed saving comes from the idle utilization seen in the lookback window instead of the price gap between the two SKUs
The listed saving is only produced for virtual machines that Advisor proposes to shut down, never for resize recommendations

explanation.correct: Advisor works out savings with retail rates and does not factor in Reserved Instances or Savings plan purchases, nor any temporary or long-term discounts. Because the compute cost here is already covered by Reserved Instances, the realized reduction after the resize is much smaller than 412 USD, and in some cross-series cases following the advice can even raise cost.

perChoice.b: It is the opposite: the recommendation does not account for Reserved Instances or Savings plan purchases at all, so that coverage is not deducted from the displayed figure.
perChoice.c: The displayed figure reflects the cost difference between the current and recommended SKUs, not how idle the workload happened to be during the lookback window.
perChoice.d: Advisor displays an estimated saving for resize recommendations as well as for shutdown recommendations, so this is not a shutdown-only figure.

body.stem: You want a budget threshold to trigger an action group that posts to a webhook and starts an automation runbook. You create the budget at the management group level, and when you open that budget for editing the control for attaching an action group is disabled. You need to explain the disabled control to the finance team. Why is it unavailable?

options.text: Action groups can be attached to budgets only at the subscription and resource group scopes
Action groups can be attached to budgets only at the management group scope
Action groups can be attached to budgets only at the billing account and enrollment account scopes
Action groups can be attached to budgets only at the billing profile and invoice section scopes

explanation.correct: Attaching an action group while you create or edit a budget is limited to subscription and resource group scopes. Because this budget sits at the management group level, the portal disables that control. Moving the budget to one of the supported scopes, or attaching the action group logic elsewhere, resolves it.

perChoice.b: The opposite is true: action group support for budgets is not offered at the management group scope, which is why the control is disabled.
perChoice.c: Billing account and enrollment account scopes are valid scopes for budgets in an Enterprise Agreement, but action groups are not offered when budgets are created or edited at those levels.
perChoice.d: Billing profile and invoice section scopes are supported budget scopes under a Microsoft Customer Agreement, but they don't support attaching an action group to a budget.

body.stem: Your tenant holds the four subscriptions listed below, and the finance team wants the same threshold-based notification configured on every one of them. You need to pick a single cost alert type that works for all four. Which cost alert type should you configure?

rows: Message when spending hits the limit the alert compares against
Message when spending hits the limit the alert compares against
Message when spending hits the limit the alert compares against
Message when spending hits the limit the alert compares against

options.text: Budget alerts
Credit alerts
Department spending quota alerts
Cost anomaly alerts

explanation.correct: Budget alerts are supported for all three Microsoft offer categories: Enterprise Agreement, Microsoft Customer Agreement, and Web direct/Pay-As-You-Go. They are generated automatically when spending based on usage or cost reaches or exceeds the amount defined in the alert condition, which matches the notification the team wants on every subscription listed.

perChoice.b: Credit alerts are available only with an Enterprise Agreement, so sub-analytics and sub-web could not receive them. They also fire at 90% and 100% of the Azure Prepayment balance rather than at a limit you choose.
perChoice.c: Department spending quota alerts are an Enterprise Agreement-only feature, so the subscriptions under the Microsoft Customer Agreement and Web direct/Pay-As-You-Go offers are not covered.
perChoice.d: Cost anomaly alerts notify you when an anomaly is detected in consumption; they are not the threshold-based alert the team is asking for on every subscription.

body.stem: You are setting up alerts on a new budget for a subscription in the portal. You need the alert configuration to be accepted exactly as you enter it, so the finance team hears from you before spending runs away. Which candidate should you submit?

options.text: Candidate A — a single actual cost threshold of 80% and one recipient email address
Candidate B — three actual cost thresholds of 50%, 80% and 120%, with no recipient email address
Candidate C — a single actual cost threshold of 2500% and one recipient email address
Candidate D — a forecast-based alert with no threshold value and one recipient email address

explanation.correct: A budget must carry at least one cost threshold, expressed as a percentage of the budget amount, together with a matching recipient email address, and alert thresholds are only supported from 0.01% to 1000%. Candidate A supplies exactly that: an in-range actual cost threshold of 80% plus an address to notify, so the portal accepts the configuration.

perChoice.b: Three thresholds are within the allowed maximum of five per budget, but no recipient email address is supplied. Because a threshold needs a corresponding address to notify, this configuration can't be accepted as entered.
perChoice.c: The threshold is 2500% of the budget amount, far above the supported ceiling of 1000% for budget alerts. The presence of a valid address doesn't make an out-of-range value acceptable.
perChoice.d: A forecast-based alert only fires when predicted spend crosses a configured threshold, so leaving the threshold value unset gives Cost Management no condition to evaluate. At least one threshold and a corresponding email address are still required.

body.stem: The administrators of a subscription are listed below. Priya, who owns the subscription, is away for two weeks and the finance director has approved a higher monthly limit for the budget she created. You need Sam, the platform engineer, to make that adjustment in place. Which statement is accurate?

options.text: Yes — a Cost Management Contributor can change the amount of a budget another user created
No — a Cost Management Contributor can change the amount only of a budget they created themselves
No — a Cost Management Contributor can see budgets in the portal but cannot change any amount
Yes — a Cost Management Contributor can delete a budget another user created and create a replacement

explanation.correct: Budgets in Cost Management follow defined role behavior: Contributor and Cost Management Contributor can create, change, or delete their own budgets, and they can change the budget amount on budgets that other people created. Sam's role therefore lets Sam raise the amount on Priya's budget without deleting and recreating it.

perChoice.b: That describes the rights over a user's own budgets. It isn't the whole picture: the same role may also change the amount on budgets created by other users, which is exactly what Sam needs here.
perChoice.c: Read-only visibility is what Reader and Cost Management Reader get on budgets they have permission to view. Cost Management Contributor has write access, so this restriction doesn't apply to Sam.
perChoice.d: Deleting is limited to a user's own budgets; removing a budget created by someone else is an Owner-level operation. That is why Sam must edit in place rather than replace it.

body.stem: You are tuning the virtual machine right-sizing recommendations that Advisor produces for the sub-core-prod subscription. You want the team's list to show only machines with low average CPU utilization, and the platform team is asking what this setting really does and how soon it takes effect. Which statement is accurate?

rows: VM/VMSS right sizing average CPU utilization filter

options.text: The setting hides recommendations outside the chosen utilization level without changing how they are generated, and it can take up to 24 hours to be reflected
The setting changes the utilization data Advisor uses to generate recommendations, and it can take up to 24 hours to be reflected
The setting hides recommendations outside the chosen utilization level without changing how they are generated, and it can take up to 48 hours to be reflected
The setting changes the utilization data Advisor uses to generate recommendations, and it can take up to 48 hours to be reflected

explanation.correct: The per-subscription average CPU utilization rule is a display filter: it limits which right-sizing recommendations you see but leaves the way Advisor generates them unchanged, and after you select a value and apply it, the new setting can take up to 24 hours to be reflected in recommendations.

perChoice.b: It does not alter the utilization data Advisor collects or the logic that produces recommendations. Changing that generation behavior isn't what this per-subscription rule does, although the 24-hour timing is right.
perChoice.c: The filtering behavior is right, but the delay belongs to a different setting. Changing the lookback period can take up to 48 hours to update recommendations; the average CPU utilization rule you are setting here reflects in up to 24 hours.
perChoice.d: Both halves are off: the rule filters the displayed recommendations without changing how they're generated, and it reflects in up to 24 hours, not 48 hours.

body.stem: You are setting up notifications for four subscriptions that sit under different agreements. Each row of the table below describes something the owning team wants to hear about. Drag each alert type to the subscription whose row it answers.

rows: The organization's remaining Azure Prepayment is running low
One cost center has used 55% of the ceiling assigned to it
Yesterday's consumption was nothing like this workload's usual pattern
Charges for the subscription reached 85% of the amount set for it

slots.label: contoso-platform-prod
fabrikam-data-prod
northwind-dev-subscription
tailspin-platform-prod

explanation.correct: contoso-platform-prod needs a Credit alert, which is raised automatically at 90% and at 100% of the remaining Azure Prepayment and is reserved for organizations on an Enterprise Agreement. fabrikam-data-prod needs a Department spending quota alert, which notifies department owners when a cost center reaches a fixed threshold of its quota (for example 50% or 75%). northwind-dev-subscription needs a Cost anomaly alert, created so you are notified automatically when an anomaly in consumption is detected. tailspin-platform-prod needs a Budget alert, raised automatically when spending, based on usage or cost, reaches or exceeds the amount defined in the budget's alert conditions.

perChoice.budget-alert: Belongs on tailspin-platform-prod: budget alerts are generated automatically whenever the alert conditions defined in a budget are met, and they are supported for all three agreement types.
perChoice.credit-alert: Belongs on contoso-platform-prod: credit alerts tell you when your Azure Prepayment is consumed and are generated automatically at 90% and 100% of the credit balance.
perChoice.department-alert: Belongs on fabrikam-data-prod: department spending quota alerts notify you when spending in a department reaches a fixed threshold of the quota set for it, such as 50% or 75%, and they are supported only on Enterprise Agreements.
perChoice.anomaly-alert: Belongs on northwind-dev-subscription: a cost anomaly alert is set up to notify you automatically when an anomaly is detected in resource consumption, which matches the row describing consumption that deviates from the normal pattern.

body.stem: Your team is rolling out a consistent approach to budgets across the tenant. Each item below is a configuration choice or situation encountered while a budget is being prepared. Drag each one to the behavior that follows from it.

items.text: The reset period is set to Quarterly
An expiration date in the future is set
The subscriptions under the management group bill in different currencies
An action group is attached to a budget created at subscription scope
Five cost thresholds and five contact addresses are entered

slots.label: The amount is spread evenly across the three months it covers
The same amount applies again in the next period, and the budget is deleted automatically afterwards
Notifications may never arrive, because the amounts under that level of the hierarchy cannot be evaluated together
Its configured receivers run as soon as a limit is crossed, and mobile push can be enabled there
This is the highest number allowed in one budget; adding another of either kind is rejected

explanation.correct: A quarterly reset period works like a monthly one, except the amount for the quarter is divided evenly among its three months. Because a budget resets automatically at the end of a period for the same budget amount when you select an expiration date in the future, and because a budget is automatically deleted once it expires, the expiration-date choice matches the behavior about reusing the same amount and then being deleted automatically. Budget evaluation requires that all subscriptions within the scope, such as a management group, operate under a single currency, so a scope whose subscriptions bill in different currencies is the one where notifications can go missing. Action groups are supported for subscription and resource group scopes, and an attached action group performs actions such as mobile push notifications, webhook calls, or automation runs when the budget threshold is met. Finally, a budget requires at least one cost threshold and a corresponding email address and can optionally include up to five thresholds and five email addresses, so five of each is the ceiling rather than a value that can be increased.

perChoice.actiongroup: Belongs with 'Its configured receivers run as soon as a limit is crossed...'. Action groups are currently supported for subscription and resource group scopes and perform actions such as mobile push notifications when the budget threshold is met.
perChoice.expiry: Belongs with 'The same amount applies again in the next period, and the budget is deleted automatically afterwards'. Selecting an expiration date in the future makes the budget reset at the end of each period for the same amount, and the budget is automatically deleted when it expires.
perChoice.fivethresholds: Belongs with 'This is the highest number allowed in one budget...'. A budget requires at least one cost threshold and a corresponding email address, and you can optionally include up to five thresholds and five email addresses.
perChoice.multicurrency: Belongs with 'Notifications may never arrive, because the amounts under that level of the hierarchy cannot be evaluated together'. Evaluation requires all subscriptions within the scope to operate under a single currency; multi-currency evaluation is not supported, so budget alerts may be missed.
perChoice.quarterly: Belongs with 'The amount is spread evenly across the three months it covers'. A quarterly budget behaves like a monthly one, except the amount for the quarter is divided evenly among the three months of the quarter.

body.stem: Advisor groups the suggestions for your subscriptions into five categories, and each category is aimed at a different goal. Drag each category to the goal it is meant to support.

slots.label: Ensure business-critical applications stay available and continue to run
Detect threats and weaknesses that might lead to a breach
Improve the speed at which applications respond
Reduce the overall amount of money spent on Azure resources
Reach process and workflow efficiency, resource manageability, and good deployment practices

explanation.correct: Advisor's dashboard sorts recommendations into five categories. Reliability is about ensuring and improving the continuity of business-critical applications; Security detects threats and vulnerabilities that might lead to breaches; Performance improves the speed of your applications; Cost optimizes and reduces your overall Azure spending; and Operational excellence helps achieve process and workflow efficiency, resource manageability, and deployment best practices. Each goal below therefore belongs to the category named after that same goal.

perChoice.cost: Fits 'Reduce the overall amount of money spent on Azure resources': the Cost category is about optimizing and reducing your overall Azure spending.
perChoice.opex: Fits 'Reach process and workflow efficiency, resource manageability, and good deployment practices': Operational excellence targets process and workflow efficiency, resource manageability, and deployment best practices.
perChoice.performance: Fits 'Improve the speed at which applications respond': the Performance category is intended to improve the speed of your applications.
perChoice.reliability: Fits 'Ensure business-critical applications stay available and continue to run': the Reliability category ensures and improves the continuity of business-critical applications.
perChoice.security: Fits 'Detect threats and weaknesses that might lead to a breach': the Security category detects threats and vulnerabilities that might lead to breaches.

body.stem: Your platform team reviews the machine-sizing suggestions Advisor produces for virtual machines and virtual machine scale sets. Each slot below describes the signal behind one of those suggestions. Drag each suggestion to the signal that produces it.

slots.label: The machine ran no activity at all over the last seven days, judged on processor and outbound network metrics
The current load still fits on a cheaper size, possibly in a newer version or a different family
Fewer machines on the same size would carry the load, and this change is preferred over changing the size itself
Average processor use sits below a specialized tier's baseline and its credits would cover the workload over seven days

explanation.correct: A shutdown recommendation is made for resources that weren't used at all over the last seven days, and its criteria are based on processor and outbound network utilization, so it belongs with the idle-machine signal. A resize SKU recommendation is made when the current load can fit on a more appropriate, less expensive size, which may be in the same family (for example D3v2 to D2v2), a newer version (D3v2 to D2v3), or a different family (D3v2 to E3v2). An instance count recommendation applies to virtual machine scale sets where fewer machines of the same SKU would carry the load; Advisor prioritizes these over SKU change recommendations because they are easily actionable and deliver faster savings. A burstable recommendation is made when average processor utilization is below a burstable SKU's baseline performance and the burstable SKU credits would be sufficient to support the average utilization over seven days.

perChoice.burstable: Belongs with 'Average processor use sits below a specialized tier's baseline...'. A burstable recommendation is issued when the average CPU utilization is less than a burstable SKU's baseline performance, P95 of CPU is under twice that baseline, the current SKU has no accelerated networking, and the burstable credits would cover average utilization over seven days.
perChoice.instancecount: Belongs with 'Fewer machines on the same size would carry the load...'. For virtual machine scale sets Advisor suggests a lower number of machines of the same SKU when that is the best fit, and it prioritizes instance count recommendations over SKU change recommendations because they are easily actionable and produce faster savings.
perChoice.resize: Belongs with 'The current load still fits on a cheaper size...'. Advisor recommends resizing a virtual machine when the current load fits on a more appropriate and less expensive SKU, which may be in the same family, a newer version, or a different family.
perChoice.shutdown: Belongs with 'The machine ran no activity at all over the last seven days...'. A shutdown recommendation is created for resources that weren't used at all over the last seven days, using processor and outbound network utilization as the criteria; memory isn't considered.

body.stem: Your team is reviewing a list of Advisor recommendations and recording an outcome for each one it looks at. Drag each status to the situation in which a reviewer sets it.

slots.label: Hide a suggestion for now because the work can't be done yet
Record that a suggestion doesn't apply in this environment
Set after carrying out the suggested change by hand, and then shown in the list with its own label
The state a suggestion starts in, and the one it returns to when someone brings it back

explanation.correct: While a recommendation is active you can update its state to manage your work: Postponed temporarily hides it so you can review it later; Dismissed indicates the recommendation isn't relevant; Completed indicates that you took the recommended action, with recommendations you complete manually shown as "Marked completed"; and Active is the state a recommendation is in before any manual change, which is also the state it returns to when a reviewer reactivates a recommendation. You can move back and forth between these states until Advisor performs system verification.

perChoice.active: Belongs with 'The state a suggestion starts in, and the one it returns to when someone brings it back'. You can change states between active, postponed, dismissed, and completed, or reactivate a recommendation, so a suggestion returns to this state when it is brought back.
perChoice.completed: Belongs with 'Set after carrying out the suggested change by hand...'. Completed indicates that you took the recommended action, and recommendations you mark as completed yourself are indicated as "Marked completed" until Advisor verifies them.
perChoice.dismissed: Belongs with 'Record that a suggestion doesn't apply in this environment'. Dismissed indicates that the recommendation isn't relevant, which is what the team means when a suggestion doesn't apply to their environment.
perChoice.postponed: Belongs with 'Hide a suggestion for now because the work can't be done yet'. Postponed temporarily hides the recommendation so you can review it later.

body.stem: You are triaging the machine-sizing suggestions Advisor has produced for the workloads listed below. Each workload owner needs to hear which of the candidate actions applies to their workload. Drag each action to the workload it belongs to.

rows: No traffic recorded over the last seven days. P95 of the maximum CPU summed across all cores: 1.8%. P100 of average CPU in the last three days: 1.5%. Outbound network utilization over a seven-day period: 0.4%.

Average CPU utilization is below the baseline performance of a B-series size. P95 of CPU is less than two times that baseline. Accelerated networking is not enabled. B-series credits are sufficient to cover the average CPU utilization over seven days.
Current load fits a smaller size in the same family: P95 of CPU and outbound network at 38% and P99 of memory at 55%, measured on the target configuration.
Provisioned ahead of a seasonal traffic spike expected in three weeks. Nothing else is deployed on this machine.

items.text: Stop the machine and eliminate its running cost
Move the workload to a burstable size with the same number of cores
Resize to a less expensive size that keeps the workload within its utilization targets
Leave the machine unchanged and suppress the suggestion

slots.label: vm-invoice01 — advised action
vm-batch07 — advised action
sc-report02 — advised action
vm-web09 — advised action

explanation.correct: The four workloads show four different patterns described in the Advisor cost recommendations for virtual machines and virtual machine scale sets: an unused machine that qualifies for a stop suggestion (vm-invoice01), a workload that meets all four documented conditions for moving to a burstable size (vm-batch07), a workload that fits a cheaper size in the same family while staying under the user-facing utilization targets (sc-report02), and a machine deliberately provisioned for expected future traffic, which is one of the documented cases where the suggestion should not be acted on (vm-web09).

perChoice.a: Belongs to vm-invoice01. A stop recommendation is produced for resources with no usage over the last seven days when the P95 of maximum CPU summed across cores is under 3%, the P100 of average CPU over the last three days is 2% or less, and outbound network utilization stays under 2% over the seven-day period. This workload's figures meet all of those conditions, so advising the owner to stop the machine and remove its running cost is the action the guidance supports.
perChoice.b: Belongs to vm-batch07. A burstable recommendation is made when average CPU is below the burstable baseline, P95 of CPU is less than twice that baseline, accelerated networking is not enabled on the current size because burstable sizes do not support it, and the burstable credits can cover the average CPU utilization over seven days. This workload matches every one of those conditions, and the resulting suggestion is to move to a burstable size keeping the same core count.
perChoice.c: Belongs to sc-report02. A smaller-size suggestion is made when the workload still meets its utilization targets on the target size: for a user-facing workload, P95 of CPU and outbound network at 40% or lower and P99 of memory at 60% or lower, with the target also cheaper, supporting the same accelerated networking and premium storage capabilities, and supported in the current region. At 38% and 55%, this user-facing workload fits a smaller size in the same family, so resizing is the correct action.
perChoice.d: Belongs to vm-web09. A machine provisioned to accommodate upcoming traffic is listed among the cases where the sizing suggestion cannot be adopted or does not apply. In those cases the documented handling is to use the dismiss or postpone option rather than act on the suggestion, so leaving the machine unchanged and suppressing the suggestion is right.

body.stem: Your team is creating a budget in the Azure portal for a subscription that tracks one line of business. The finance team wants to hear from the service itself as spending climbs toward the agreed limit, so the notification settings must be accepted exactly as they are typed in.
body.statement: Enter {{threshold}} as the smallest percentage of the budget amount a cost threshold can be set to, and enter {{count}} as the largest number of thresholds and contact email addresses a single budget supports.

options.text: One threshold and one email address
Five thresholds and five email addresses
Three thresholds and three email addresses
Ten thresholds and ten email addresses

explanation.correct: The alert limit for a budget supports a range of 0.01% to 1000% of the budget threshold, so 0.01% is the smallest cost threshold the portal accepts. A budget requires at least one cost threshold with a matching email address, and you can optionally include up to five thresholds and five email addresses in a single budget, so five of each is the maximum.

perChoice.threshold:b: 0.001% sits below the documented range, whose lower bound is 0.01% of the budget threshold, so the portal would reject it.
perChoice.threshold:c: 1% is inside the supported range, but it is not the smallest value a threshold can be set to.
perChoice.threshold:d: 10% is accepted as a threshold value, but again it is not the lowest value in the supported range.
perChoice.count:a: A budget can carry more than one threshold and more than one contact, so this understates what the service supports.
perChoice.count:c: Three of each is allowed, but the documented ceiling per budget is five thresholds and five email addresses.
perChoice.count:d: Ten of each is well beyond what a single budget supports, so the configuration would be rejected.

body.stem: Your finance team bought reserved capacity and a savings plan for a subscription, and both purchases were charged in full in a single month. The budget emails for that subscription report far less than the totals on the invoice, and the team wants to know why. Which statement accounts for the difference?

rows: 12,000 in full, booked in one month
6,000 in full, booked in one month

options.text: Evaluations use actual cost and don't include amortization
Evaluations use actual cost and include amortization
Evaluations use amortized cost and include amortization
Evaluations use amortized cost and don't include amortization

explanation.correct: Budget cost evaluations are based on actual cost and explicitly don't include amortization. Reserved instance and purchase data are now part of what budgets evaluate, but the purchase is counted at its actual amount in the period it lands rather than being spread across the covered term, so the totals behind the budget emails are lower than the amortized view finance expects.

perChoice.basis:b: Amortization is never part of a budget evaluation, so pairing it with actual cost is not correct.
perChoice.basis:c: Budgets don't spread a purchase across its term, so neither half of this statement matches how evaluations work.
perChoice.basis:d: The second half is right, but evaluations aren't amortized; they are calculated from actual cost.

body.stem: Your organization holds an Enterprise Agreement, and its Azure Prepayment is being consumed faster than the finance director expected as new environments are provisioned. Nobody wants to maintain a budget for this agreement, but the director does want an automatic notification as the balance is drawn down, at the points the service itself uses. Which arrangement delivers that?
body.statement: Configure {{alertType}} for the agreement, and expect the service to notify the account owners at {{levels}} of the Azure Prepayment balance.

options.text: Budget alert
Credit alert
Department spending quota alert
Cost anomaly alert

explanation.correct: Cost Management generates credit alerts automatically at 90% and at 100% of the organization's Azure Prepayment balance, which is the offering for organizations with an Enterprise Agreement. Each notification is reflected in the cost alerts list and emailed to the account owners, so no budget has to be maintained.

perChoice.alertType:a: Budget alerts only fire when spending reaches a threshold someone defined on a budget, so they don't track consumption of the Azure Prepayment.
perChoice.alertType:c: Department spending quota alerts depend on a spending quota configured in the portal and go to department owners; they are a different mechanism.
perChoice.alertType:d: A cost anomaly alert reports unusual consumption patterns that Cost Management detects; it doesn't report progress against the Azure Prepayment balance.
perChoice.levels:a: These figures resemble the kind of levels configured for department spending quotas, not the automatic points used for this alert type.
perChoice.levels:b: 90% appears, but the service pairs it with a different second level, so this pair is not what it uses.
perChoice.levels:c: Neither of these levels is one of the automatic trigger points for this alert type.

body.stem: Your platform team works through the items listed in the Advisor dashboard. For one recommendation, a reviewer changed its state to completed by hand because the fix had already been applied outside the portal, and Advisor has not yet confirmed the change. You need to set the team's expectations about what happens next. Which statement is accurate?
body.statement: Advisor can take {{time}} to recognize that the action was taken, and until it does, a recommendation a reviewer completed by hand is displayed as {{label}}.

options.text: up to 24 hours
up to 48 hours
up to one hour
no time at all
Marked completed
Completed
Postponed
Dismissed

explanation.correct: After you implement a recommendation, it can take up to a day, that is up to 24 hours, for Advisor to recognize the action and run its system verification. Until that verification takes place, a recommendation that a reviewer completed by hand is shown with the indication 'Marked completed', which distinguishes it from one Advisor verified on its own.

perChoice.time:b: The 48-hour window belongs to the lookback period setting for virtual machine right-sizing recommendations; after that configuration changes, recommendations may take up to 48 hours to refresh. It isn't the delay for recognizing an implemented action.
perChoice.time:c: An hour is roughly how long a budget threshold notification takes after an evaluation, which is unrelated to Advisor verifying an implemented recommendation.
perChoice.time:d: Advisor does perform system verification itself and updates the state once it does, so the action isn't recognized with no delay.
perChoice.label:b: 'Completed' is the state Advisor assigns after its own system verification succeeds; a state set by hand is displayed with a separate indication.
perChoice.label:c: Postponed means the reviewer intends to review the recommendation again later.
perChoice.label:d: Dismissed means the reviewer has decided the recommendation isn't relevant.

body.stem: Your tenant's management group holds subscriptions denominated in euros and others denominated in US dollars. The finance lead created a budget at that management group level, and the notifications configured on it never arrive. You need to restore them without changing the spending limit the team agreed on.
body.statement: Choose {{fix}} so that the finance lead starts receiving the notifications again.

options.text: Narrow the budget to a scope whose subscriptions all use one currency
Add another budget at the same management group scope for subscriptions in the second currency
Change the reset period of the existing budget at that scope to the billing quarter
Add filters for publisher type Azure and charge type Usage to the existing budget at that scope

explanation.correct: For budget evaluation, all subscriptions inside the scope, such as a management group, must operate under a single currency. Multi-currency evaluation isn't supported, which is why the notifications for the management group budget are missed. Placing the budget on a scope whose subscriptions all use one currency restores the evaluation and its alerts.

perChoice.fix:b: Adding a second budget at the same management group scope doesn't resolve anything: the limitation applies to the subscriptions inside the scope, not to the number of budgets defined there.
perChoice.fix:c: The reset period only controls how the amount is divided across the months of a period; it has no bearing on the mixed currencies of the subscriptions being evaluated.
perChoice.fix:d: Those filters restrict which charges count toward the evaluation, limiting it to first-party Azure consumption, but they don't address the mixed currencies that stop the notifications from being produced.

body.stem: Your team defined the budget shown below for the sub-prod-web subscription, and the finance director now wants a higher monthly limit to take effect next January. You need to tell the team what happens to this budget as time passes and what they would have to do to put the higher limit into effect. Which statement is accurate?
body.statement: Because this budget {{reset}} at the end of each period, you must {{change}} to apply a different limit from January, and when its expiration date arrives the budget {{expiry}}.

options.text: resets with the same amount
resets with the latest forecast
resets with the highest month's cost
keeps its amount until edited by hand
create a separate budget
edit the limit on this budget

add another alert threshold
is deleted automatically
keeps evaluating at the last limit
stays in place until deleted by hand

explanation.correct: A budget that has a future expiration date resets at the end of every monthly, quarterly, or annual period for the same budget amount, so the cost being evaluated starts again from zero against the identical figure. Because it always comes back with the same value, changing the amount that applies to later periods means putting in a new budget rather than adjusting the existing one. Once the expiration date passes, the budget is automatically deleted rather than left in place.

perChoice.reset:b: The carried-over figure is not recalculated from a forecast. Forecasted cost predictions are used only to decide when forecasted alerts fire; the budget still returns to the amount that was entered.
perChoice.reset:c: Spending recorded earlier in the period does not change what the budget returns to. Only the accumulated cost restarts from zero, against the same budget figure each time.
perChoice.reset:d: No manual step is needed at a period boundary. The budget returns to the same figure by itself, and it stops being evaluated only when its expiration date is reached.
perChoice.change:b: Editing affects what the existing budget measures against while it remains in place, but each new period starts again with that same figure, so the edit does not carry a different value into future periods.
perChoice.change:c: Ending a period does not substitute a new figure. The following period starts again from the same value, so waiting never puts the higher limit in effect.
perChoice.change:d: Thresholds only govern when notifications are sent; they do not alter the amount that spending is measured against.
perChoice.expiry:b: Evaluation of costs stops when the expiration date is reached. The budget does not keep running against its last limit after that date.
perChoice.expiry:c: No manual removal is required. When the expiration date arrives the budget is removed on its own, so there is nothing left to delete by hand.
perChoice.expiry:d: A budget stays attached to the scope it was defined on for its whole life; expiration does not relocate or duplicate it to a parent scope.
